title: Persistent dry cough on blood pressure tablets

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hello, Mr Penhaligon, come in and have a seat. And you've brought someone with you?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My wife, Margaret. She does the remembering.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Someone has to.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Lovely to meet you both. So what can I do for you today?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It's this cough. It's driving me mad. Dry, tickly, it never stops.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How long has it been going on?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: About six weeks now.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: It's longer than that, Geoff. It started before your sister's birthday, and that was early August.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, she's right. More like two months, then.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay, so about two months. Are you bringing anything up when you cough?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, nothing. It's completely dry.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any blood at all?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any fevers, night sweats, or losing weight?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. If anything I've put a bit on.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any breathlessness or chest pain?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, I'm fine walking the dog. No chest pain.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any heartburn, or acid coming up into your throat?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any change in your voice, or trouble swallowing?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, nothing like that.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Do you smoke, or have you ever smoked?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I gave up twenty years ago. Before that I smoked about ten a day, for maybe fifteen years.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thank you. And I can see from your record we started you on ramipril for your blood pressure. When was that?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Back in the summer. June?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: It was the end of May. I remember because we'd just come back from Whitby.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: End of May, then.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And what dose are you taking now?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Ten milligrams. Hang on, let me look at the box. No, it's five. Five milligrams, once a day. They put it up from two and a half in July.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That's really helpful, thank you. Any other medicines?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Just atorvastatin, twenty milligrams at night.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any allergies to medicines?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: None that I know of.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I'm the one who coughs at night as well, but mine's my asthma. Don't go putting that in his notes!

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'll make sure only Geoff's chest goes in Geoff's notes. Geoff, have you ever had asthma yourself?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, never.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Let me have a listen to your chest. Deep breaths in and out through your mouth. That sounds clear on both sides. Open wide for me. Your throat looks normal. And let me check your blood pressure. It's 134 over 82.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's better than it was.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: It is. The ramipril is doing its job for your blood pressure. But I think the ramipril is also what's causing the cough. It's a well-known side effect of that group of medicines, and the timing fits: the cough started after you began it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Really? I thought I'd picked something up.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Nothing you've told me points to an infection, and your chest sounds clear. What I'd suggest is we stop the ramipril and switch you to a different tablet called losartan, which works in a similar way but doesn't usually cause a cough.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. What dose would that be?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: We'll start at fifty milligrams once a day. I'd like a blood test to check your kidneys and salt levels one to two weeks after you start it, and I'll see you again in four weeks to check your blood pressure.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Will the cough go straight away?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Not always. It can take a few weeks, sometimes up to three months, to settle after stopping ramipril.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Because you used to smoke and the cough has gone on for a couple of months, I'd also like to arrange a chest X-ray, just to be thorough. It's very likely to be normal.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: If you cough up any blood, become short of breath, lose weight without trying, or get any chest pain, I want you to contact us sooner and not wait for the appointment.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I'll keep an eye on him.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And if the cough hasn't improved at all by the four-week review, we'll think again about other causes.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thanks, doctor.

reference_note.history: Persistent dry, tickly, non-productive cough. No haemoptysis. No fevers, night sweats or weight loss. No breathlessness or chest pain. No heartburn. No voice change or dysphagia. Ramipril started end of May for hypertension, increased from 2.5 mg to 5 mg in July; cough began after starting ramipril. Ex-smoker: stopped 20 years ago, previously 10 per day for about 15 years (approximately 7.5 pack-years). No history of asthma. Attended with wife.
reference_note.medications_allergies: Ramipril 5 mg once daily. Atorvastatin 20 mg at night. No known drug allergies.
reference_note.examination: Chest clear bilaterally. Throat normal. BP 134/82.
reference_note.impression: Persistent dry cough, most likely ACE inhibitor induced. Hypertension well controlled on ramipril.
reference_note.plan: Stop ramipril. Start losartan 50 mg once daily. U&Es 1–2 weeks after starting losartan. Chest X-ray (ex-smoker, cough for 2 months). Review in 4 weeks with blood pressure check. Advised the cough may take up to 3 months to resolve after stopping ramipril. If no improvement at review, consider other causes.
reference_note.safety_netting: Contact the practice sooner if haemoptysis, breathlessness, unintentional weight loss or chest pain.

mutations.seeded_rationale: The patient corrected 10 mg to 5 mg after checking the box; ramipril is being stopped, so harm is limited to a misleading medication history.
mutations.description: Ramipril dose kept at the figure the patient corrected

mutations.seeded_rationale: The wife's asthma recorded as the patient's may lead to the cough being attributed to asthma and to inappropriate inhaler or beta-blocker decisions in future.
mutations.description: Wife's asthma recorded as the patient's

mutations.seeded_rationale: Renal function and potassium monitoring after starting an angiotensin receptor blocker would be missed, risking undetected hyperkalaemia or kidney injury.
mutations.description: Kidney blood test after the switch deferred to annual review

mutations.seeded_rationale: A 2-week cough falls below the 3-week threshold for chest X-ray in an ex-smoker over 40 (NICE NG12), so the X-ray may be cancelled or deprioritised.
mutations.description: Cough duration shortened from two months to two weeks

mutations.original_text: Contact the practice sooner if haemoptysis, breathlessness, unintentional weight loss or chest pain.
mutations.seeded_rationale: Red-flag advice about haemoptysis and weight loss was given verbally but is undocumented, so it will not be reinforced and its absence is medicolegally significant.
Twice-daily dosing doubles the intended starting dose, increasing the risk of hypotension, falls and hyperkalaemia.
Who attended is useful context but does not change management.
